Vṛtragītā
(‘the teaching [given to] Vṛtra [by the sage सनक]’)
------------------------------------------
This is one of the minor Gītās that appears in the Mahābhārata (Śāntiparva 279 and 280; 104 ślokas).
Vṛtra, the king of the दानवस् or असुरस् (demons) asked his गुरु Śukrā-cārya about the secret of कर्म and its resultant births. When शुक्राचार्य was about to answer, Sanatkumāra, the great sage arrived there. He was requested to answer the questions.
The discourse of Sanatkumāra is quite long and complicated. Only the gist may be given here:
Mahāviṣṇu is the Supreme Lord who creates, sustains and then dissolves the whole च्रेअतिओन्. All the worlds and all the beings are established in him only.
The jīvas or the embodied souls pass through the rounds of births and deaths because of their vāsanās (strong mental impressions) brought about by their karmas or actions, good or bad.
After experiencing the result of their karmas in higher worlds like हेअवेन् or lower worlds like हेल्ल्, they return to the world of men. If they perform spiritual sādhanas and realise their true nature as आत्मन्, they will attain the supreme world of विष्णु.
Vṛtra realised it by the grace of Mahāviṣṇu and got लिबेरतिओन्.

vṛtti
------------------------------------------
This word, though it appears to be very simple, has as many as fourteen meanings or senses! Only a few of them can be given here.
It means a vocation by which a person earns his livelihood.
In Sanskrit literature, it stands for a simple commentary on a well-known treatise, especially in the form of sūtras.
In the Yogasūtras (1.2, 4, 5, 10) it stands for the modifications of the मिन्द्.
In drama literature, it signifies a sentiment.
It may also mean behaviour in general.

Vṛtrāsura
------------------------------------------
The story of Vṛtra or वृत्रासुर is as old as the Ṛgveda (vide 1.32.5). There, Vṛtra is pictured as the demon of drought preventing rain-bearing clouds from giving rain. इन्द्र ‘kills’ him with his वज्र or वज्रायुध (thunderbolt) and releases the water.
In the पुराणस् he is described as the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, created out of sacrificial fire, to destroy इन्द्र who had earlier killed विश्वरूप, the first son of Tvaṣṭṛ. A mistake in the chanting of the Vedic मन्त्र during the pouring of oblations resulted in वृत्रासुर becoming vulnerable to इन्द्र’s weapon. Though वृत्रासुर conquered इन्द्र first he was later killed by the latter.
Vṛtrāsura was a king, Citraketu by name, in his previous birth. He was a great devotee of विष्णु (vide Bhāgavata 6.11).
See DADHĪCI also.
